posts.title: When Two Versions of the Law Disagree

origin.label: The story on Tech From Here: Hawaiʻi

images.what: A black-and-white photograph from about 1870 of Aliʻiōlani Hale in Honolulu, a two-story stone government building with a clock tower and a tall flagpole in an open yard. It was the Kingdom government building that later housed its Legislature and Supreme Court
images.credit: Photo: HABS / Hawaii State Archives, PD

images.what: Page 6 of the Compiler's Preface to the 1846 Statute Laws, in old printed type. It says the code went to the king's cabinet for discussion, then to the Rev. William Richards for faithful translation into the native language, then to both houses for three readings, debated section by section

Page 259 of volume 1 of the Hawaiian Reports, headed 1856, Hardy vs. Ruggles, in old printed type. The lines read that where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian, the latter must govern, because it is the language of the legislators of the country

Page 367 of the 1859 Civil Code, Chapter XLI, General Provisions, in old printed type. Section 1493 says that if a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian versions of any part of the Code, the English version shall be held binding. The page ends with the approval of May 17, 1859, signed Kamehameha

Four lines of old printed type from the same page of Hardy v. Ruggles. They read that the English and Hawaiian may often be used to help and explain each other where the meaning is obscure, or the contradiction slight, but where the omission in the Hawaiian is clear, it is impossible to reconcile them

A printed act headed An Act for the Construction of Statutes Where the English and Hawaiian Versions Do Not Agree. Its one section says that whenever a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian version of any of the laws of the Kingdom, which have been, or may hereafter be enacted, the English version shall be held binding. Approved January 10, 1865, signed Kamehameha R.
images.credit: Source: Laws of 1864 to 1865, p. 68, PD

images.what: A 1943 session-law page headed Promulgation of Laws. Act 218 rewrites the rule so that the secretary of the Territory publishes the laws once in the English language in a Honolulu daily newspaper. The Hawaiian-language publication is gone from the text

Two crops of a 1979 session-law page, Act 97, S.B. No. 45. It rewrites section 1-13: English and Hawaiian are the official languages of Hawaii; where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian version of any state law, the English version shall be held binding; Hawaiian shall not be required for public acts and transactions

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 16, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined new text adds a proviso to section 1-13: if a law was originally drafted in Hawaiian and its English version was translated from it, and the law has not been subsequently amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English, the Hawaiian version shall be held binding

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 109, S.D. 2, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined text adds the same proviso for laws originally drafted in Hawaiian and not later amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English. Its last line reads: This Act shall take effect on July 1, 3000

A typed bill page, H.B. No. 2433, H.D. 1, S.D. 1, with numbered lines. The sentence making the English version binding is struck through. New underlined text gives priority to the language that aligns with the intent of the legislature as evidenced by legislative history, context and purpose. The last line sets the effective date at March 22, 2075

Seven lines of old printed type from page 480 of volume 8 of the Hawaiian Reports, April 1892, In re Ross. They read that the English version shall be held binding, that the two versions constitute but one act, that there is no dual legislation, and that as a rule one version is the translation of the other

The top of page 69 of volume 2 of the Hawaiian Reports, 1858, Levi Haalelea v. Daniel Montgomery, in old printed type. It reads that the deed is a printed formula in two languages, that the English version of this formula is, of course, the original, and the Hawaiian merely a translation

posts.title: The Lines That Changed the Land

origin.label: The story on Tech From Here: Hawaiʻi

other.label: State land survey division digitizing maps to help public (ags.hawaii.gov)

images.what: A handwritten Land Commission award-book page of October 12, 1850: a pen-and-ink plat of a parcel with a creek along one edge, hachured hillside and neighboring-land names, the tail of a courses-and-distances description above it, a costs list and the commissioners' signatures below. It is an actual parcel made legible as a drawing, a description and a signed document, which is the sentence this story opens with

A handwritten Land Commission page signed by surveyor A. F. Turner in July 1850: a description of a Honolulu lot that starts at the corner of Nuuanu and King Streets and runs by bearings and chain lengths to the point of commencement, with a hand-drawn plat showing the Bethel Chapel and neighboring lots beside it. It shows a boundary put into words, measured and drawn on one page

The top of a handwritten Hawaiian-language page in the first Land Commission award book, under the names of three commissioners, J. Y. Kanehoa, John ʻĪʻī and Z. Kaauwai. It says the notice ran in the Polynesian newspaper on February 14, 1846, and it is headed as a notice to everyone holding a land right across the Hawaiian islands. It is the commission's call for written claims, the thing a claimant presented in place of the land

A handwritten Land Commission award-book page of October 27, 1852, headed with an award number (Helu 570B), with two ʻāpana described by bearings and distances and signed by surveyor S. P. Kalama, two hand-drawn plats of the parcels at the bottom, and the commissioners' signatures with the fee line at the top. It shows the pieces the card lists: an award number, a survey and a metes-and-bounds description on one document

a rusted metal target on a post set in a mortared lava-rock pier, a Hawaii Territorial Survey triangulation station called LUKE, with the Wailuku valley and clouded mountains behind it. It shows a physical mark left by Hawaiian land surveying; it is a later Territorial-era station, not a Māhele-era survey, a metes-and-bounds description or a patent

Part of a handwritten Land Commission page for claim 539, Kukuihaa uka at Hōnaunau, Kona, Hawaiʻi: the line "The rights of Native tenants, if any, must be respected," then a boundary that starts at a rock marked with a cross on pāhoehoe lava, follows a small stone wall up to a pile of stones, and runs by bearings and chain lengths back to the start. It shows a boundary known through landmarks restated as courses and distances

A handwritten Land Commission page in Hawaiian with ruled lists of bearings and chain distances for three separate ʻāpana, the neighboring holding named at the end of each line, a handwritten column of sums in the right margin, and three hand-drawn plats with a chain scale below. It shows a description that was calculated, copied into the file and drawn

A handwritten Land Commission page from November 1853: a description of a Honolulu lot at Puaa by bearings and chain lengths signed by surveyor A. F. Turner, a hand-drawn plat with a scale of one chain to an inch, and below it the start of another award, number 7767, with a ruled fee table and the commissioners' signatures. It is the kind of award document descendants search, with its limits visible: one surveyor's lines on one date

Two surveyors, rodman Harry Kawamoto and topographer J. O. Kilmartin, standing at the Mauna Kea triangulation station on the cinder plateau of Hawaiʻi Island on October 25, 1925; the station was set by the Hawaiian Government Survey in 1892. It shows the field measurement behind the boundary lines the sentence asks readers to read first as measurements
images.credit: Photo: J. O. Kilmartin, USGS, 1925, PD

images.what: A handwritten Land Commission award-book page dated September 3, 1853: award number 4779 at Wailua, Koʻolau, Maui, a description by bearings and distances signed by surveyor A. F. Turner, a small plat of a long narrow parcel beside a stream, and the four commissioners' signatures over a paid fee. It is one of the instruments the sentence means: a signed document that holds the boundary without anyone going back to the land

research.label: File:Engineering features of the Waiahole Water Project of the Waiahole Water Co. Island of Oahu, Territory of Hawaii (IA engineeringfeatu00klue 0) (commons.wikimedia.org)

images.what: Black-and-white 1916 photograph looking down a timbered tunnel in the Waiāhole project: curved wooden arch forms overhead, a plank wall on the right and narrow rail tracks on the floor leading into the dark. The report's own caption reads 'Portion of tunnel, showing forms for arch of tunnel roof' and does not say which tunnel or heading. It opens the story inside the mountain, on the machine itself
images.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

images.what: USGS map of the Waiāhole Ditch System: a blue dotted line starts at the Kahana tunnels in the windward valleys, runs south past Waikāne and Uwao tunnels and Gates 30 and 31, passes under the Koʻolau at the North Portal, comes out past Adit 8 and crosses central Oʻahu to Reservoir 155. Black outlines mark the Kahana, Waikāne and Waiāhole watersheds the ditch draws from

Black-and-white 1916 photograph of two large riveted steel pipes arching over a cut in a hillside at Waikakalaua Gulch, with a railway track running through the cut below. The report's caption calls them steel pipes crossing a branch of the Oahu Railway, the larger one the new 72-inch pipe. They are the part of the route where the conduit crosses a gulch instead of a tunnel or ditch
images.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

images.what: First page of Act 111, Session Laws of Hawaiʻi 1998, the law that let the state buy the Waiāhole water system. Section 2 opens: Water belongs to the people and the State should be the steward in managing and ensuring the allocation of this resource for the highest and best use in the public interest

Black-and-white 1916 photograph of a worker in a hat standing before two concrete-framed gates with hand wheels above them, set into the mouth of a finished section of the conduit. The report captions it 'Gates at a section of finished conduit.' It shows the kind of gate the sentence means, the control that moves in minutes
images.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

images.what: Printed paragraph from page 111 of the 2000 Waiāhole opinion: For the reasons fully explained below, we affirm in part and vacate in part the Commission's decision and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion

The caption of the opinion as printed on page 97 of the Hawaiʻi Reports: In the Matter of the Water Use Permit Applications ... for the Waiāhole Ditch Combined Contested Case Hearing. No. 21309. Supreme Court of Hawaiʻi. Aug. 22, 2000

Letterhead of the State of Hawaiʻi Commission on Water Resource Management, dated December 24, 1997. The letter tells the parties that the Commission's Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Decision and Order for the Waiāhole Ditch Combined Contested Case Hearing are enclosed: the decision the Supreme Court later reviewed

Black-and-white 2019 photograph of two large siphon pipes crossing Kipapa Gulch side by side: on the left a newer siphon behind a concrete intake with a wooden screen, on the right the historic riveted-steel siphon behind a rusted grate. The survey caption says the historic one is no longer in use and the newer one is in use. It shows the fixed physical network of the Waiāhole Ditch carrying today's water through 1916-era works

Lines of type from page 6 of Kluegel's 1916 report: the highest intake at 790 feet, and the length of the main tunnel through the Koolau Ridge, 14,567 feet, or 2.76 miles, with the North Portal at 752 feet and the South Portal at 724 feet. The usual facts, which the slide says are not the only questions

Black-and-white 1916 photograph inside the main tunnel: a wall of dark rock with water jetting and spraying out of it into the bore, and two men with lanterns standing near the floor. The report's caption reads 'Water issuing from water-bearing rock in the main tunnel, 10,550 feet from the South Portal, March 23, 1915,' and explains that the lanterns are held by men beside a drill. It shows the mountain's own stored groundwater, the landscape process the tunnel tapped
images.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

images.what: Black-and-white 1914 photograph of six tunnel workers in work clothes and caps standing together underground in front of a rock face, with a drill rig and air hose across the foreground. The report's caption reads 'Japanese professional tunnel men, Main Tunnel, July, 1914,' and its text credits them with most of the drilling and mucking. It puts the people who built the tunnel in the frame
images.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

images.what: Paragraph from page 178 of a 1913 USGS report, written about 1911, before the ditch: Waiāhole Stream rises in springs about 1,000 feet above sea level, its flow is fairly constant, and a part of the water is used for irrigating rice and taro lands in the lower part of the valley

Typed lines from page 3 of a 2025 Hawaiʻi Senate bill on the Waiāhole water system, listing who depends on it today: Aloun Farms, the Hawaii Agriculture Research Center, Larry Jefts Farm, Mililani Nursery, Mililani Agricultural Park, Sugarland Farms, Waiawa Nursery, Waikele Farms, livestock ranchers, Mililani Memorial Park and the Waiawa correctional facility

A Parshall flume on the Waiāhole Ditch near Mililani in June 2019 (HAER HI-146-8): a concrete channel that narrows in the middle so one depth reading gives a flow rate, with smooth fast water and tall grass on the banks. By 2019 a laser sensor upstream had replaced it. It shows a gauge, the subject of the line

Page 728 of a 1921 territorial Supreme Court opinion setting out the deals made before the tunnel was dug: a fifty-year lease of Kahana's surplus water from May 27, 1916, and a December 30, 1912 deed of water rights in Kahana, Waikāne and Waiāhole for $257,500, each subject to the valley residents' water for household use and irrigation

The start of the conclusion of the 2000 Waiāhole opinion, page 189: For the reasons stated in this opinion, we vacate in part the Commission's decision and remand for additional findings and conclusions ... regarding the following, beginning with an interim instream flow standard for windward streams

Faded photograph from a 1913 USGS paper, captioned Velocity-area gaging station, Waiāhole Stream: two men measure the stream by wading it, one seated in the water and one holding a rod, while men in hats watch from the grassy bank. A flow measurement, the thing the line says cannot decide allocation on its own

A metal gate set into the concrete wall of the Waiāhole Ditch near Mililani, with a staff scale marked in one-foot steps and a narrow concrete footbridge at right, photographed for the National Park Service HAER survey in June 2019 (HAER HI-146-4). The 1916 machine still decides, gate by gate, where today's water goes
images.credit: Photo: David Franzen, HAER, Public domain

images.what: Line chart from the USGS low-flow study, Figure 34: daily water released at Gate 31 to Waiāhole Stream from January 1999 to late 2004, a jagged blue line mostly between 5 and 25 million gallons a day, above a flat pink line for the Commission's targeted restoration flow of 4, then 4.8 million gallons a day

posts.title: Kaʻena Point’s Golf Balls Helped Run America’s First Imaging Spy Satellites

origin.label: The story on Tech From Here: Hawaiʻi

research.label: 2019 06 08 OA Section 106 HULA C Bldg 35 at KPSTS (files.hawaii.gov)
2011 09 08 OA NEPA DEA Kaena Point Satellite Station Demolition Construction (files.hawaii.gov)

other.label: Kaena point satellite tracking station celebrates 55 years (dvidshub.net)
Corona americas first imaging satellite program (cia.gov)

images.what: A single white radome sits on a green ridge above the blue Pacific at Kaʻena Point Space Force Station, photographed in September 2022. It is the actual golf ball of the title, shown as it looks today, not in the CORONA era
images.credit: Photo: Brooke Wise, USSF, Public domain

images.what: A large white radome and a smaller one beside a dish antenna stand on a grassy ridge above the ocean at the Kaʻena Point Satellite Tracking Station, photographed in 2008. It shows the radomes the opening sentence describes

Typed page 10 of the federal survey of the Kaʻena Point station, HAER HI-97. It lists the land's owners from the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi to the State and the Campbell Estate, with the Army and then the Air Force as lessees from 1958, and says the original site was land leased from the Territory of Hawaiʻi and private owners, 106 acres in 1958

Typed Significance section of the federal survey, HAER HI-97 page 7. It says the station was established in 1958 to support the CORONA/Discoverer Satellite Program, that the nation's first satellite reconnaissance program was named Discoverer and became known by its codeword CORONA, and that the station, then known as HULA, supported it with data retrieval, tracking and relay

The camera system built for the Discoverer and CORONA satellites on display at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in 2012: a long metal frame holding the camera and film machinery, with the gold capsule that brought the film back to Earth at its right end. It is the system that first returned photographs from orbit

The CIA's line drawing titled Satellite Control Facility Operation in Recovery: three dashed satellite passes over Alaska, ENABLE commands from the control center and Vandenberg (STC, VTS) and a backup from Kodiak (KTS), Control arrows from the control center to the stations, and the Hawaii Tracking Station (HTS) at the bottom sending Control to a recovery plane near the capsule's impact point
images.credit: Source: CIA CORONA history, vol. 4, PD

images.what: Typed lines from page 229 of the NRO's declassification guide, section 5, Operations: MGS and RTS. Under Redact, item a reads: Redact specific details about the Mission Ground Station or Remote Tracking Station commands that were uplinked to the satellite, i.e., orbit adjustment, deorbit, camera operations, SIGINT payload operations, etc
images.credit: Source: NRO redaction guide, p. 229, PD

images.what: Typed list from page 52 of the NRO's declassification guide: Release fact that the following remote tracking stations supported DISCOVERER (CORONA) and/or SAMOS reconnaissance satellite programs, followed by ten sites from Annette Island, Alaska, to Vandenberg AFB, California, with Kaena Point, Hawaii, fourth
images.credit: Source: NRO redaction guide, p. 52, PD

images.what: Photograph of a CORONA parachute bag from the CIA Museum: an olive-green nylon pack with webbing straps and laced seams. It held the parachute that opened after the film capsule separated from the spacecraft and slowed it on the way down
A black-and-white U.S. Air Force photograph of a C-119J Flying Boxcar towing a CORONA film capsule on its parachute after a midair catch. The photo is not identified as a Hawaiʻi recovery
images.credit: Source: U.S. Air Force, Public domain

images.what: Close view of the nose, cockpit windows and left propeller of the C-119J Flying Boxcar marked 037, now at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force. It is the Hickam-based plane, Pelican 9, whose crew caught the Discoverer XIV film capsule in midair in August 1960

A CORONA recovery vehicle, the gold-colored capsule shell that carried exposed film back through re-entry, on display at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in 2008. It is one of the very different machines in the chain of custody
A CORONA film canister with its lid off and a spool of film beside it, photographed by the CIA. It is the physical object that had to move from the recovered capsule to secure processing elsewhere

The CIA's chart titled CORONA Program Synopsis: a curve of total launches rising from 1959 to 1972, labels for program firsts from First Polar Orbit and First Air Recovery to Last CORONA Series Flight, and a table at the bottom: 8 launches and no recoveries in 1959, 11 launches and 4 recoveries in 1960, and the program running to 1972. Two blank white boxes are the CIA's redactions
images.credit: Source: CIA CORONA history, vol. 1, PD

images.what: A brass CORONA retrieval hook wrapped in tape and rope, on display at the Smithsonian's Udvar-Hazy Center in Virginia in 2018. Eight hooks like it hung from a frame behind the recovery plane and snagged the capsule's parachute, the recovery step at the end of the list

Looking along the Waiʻanae coast from above Keawaʻula Bay: a sunlit slope in the foreground, the bay and cliffs to the right, and the station radomes small on the ridge at the far left, photographed in September 2022. It shows how the station sits inside a wider landscape

An aerial view of the Kaʻena Point station released for its 55th anniversary: two white radomes on the ridge, the road, a helipad and the operations building above the ocean. It shows the two sides of the station the sentence describes

images.what: A Satellite Control Network maintainer watches a monitor at Kaʻena Point Space Force Station on 13 September 2022, in an official Space Force photograph. The story refers to maintainers and a system operator named in the Space Force’s own public captions as people doing work usually hidden behind the word station
